..
Issued at 502 AM CDT Mon Sep 28 2026

Shortwave energy ejecting from the base of a deep western CONUS
trough is spreading over the Northern Plains this morning while
the low level jet advects warm air and moisture into the 
region. These forcing mechanisms are responsible for areas of 
showers and thunderstorms. At 430 AM CDT, there were two 
distinct clusters of convection: one over north central North 
Dakota and another moving into far southwest and south central 
North Dakota, both traveling northeastward. The space between 
these two areas is likely to fill in eventually, but this may 
not occur until mid to late morning over the eastern third of 
the state. SPC mesoanalysis indicates 40 to 50 kts of effective
bulk shear, but this may be too high and analyzed from the base
of an inflow layer different from that of reality. While storms
have been strong at times, would anticipate more intense and 
sustained updrafts with that amount of shear and up to 1000 J/kg
MUCAPE. Through the rest of this morning and into the 
afternoon, the broader expanse of showers and storms will 
propagate northeastward into the Red River Valley in congruence 
with a mid level shortwave and the attendant low level warm air 
advection/moisture transport. Recent guidance has trended 
towards a drier afternoon across western and central North 
Dakota, although smaller clusters of more widely scattered 
showers and storms could be maintained by mid level 
frontogenesis across the south and a poleward advancing surface 
warm front across the north. 

By early evening, the left exit region of an upper level jet 
will reach south central North Dakota over lower to mid level 
cyclogenesis adjacent to a strengthening low level jet. This is 
expected to produce another round of widespread showers and 
scattered thunderstorms across central and eastern North Dakota 
that could persist through tonight. This appears to be a 
favorable setup for training convection that could produce 
localized areas of flash flooding, with storm motion and deep 
layer wind vectors intersecting the low level jet and moisture 
transport vectors at an angle greater than 45 degrees, 
precipitable water approaching climatological maximum values, 
high deep layer RH, deep warm cloud depths, and skinny CAPE 
profiles. Nearly every CAM produces a narrow swath of at least 
3 to 5 inches of total rainfall this morning through tonight. 
The most probable area for this to occur is from the Missouri 
River south of Lake Sakakawea to the Red River Valley north of 
Fargo. But only a small fraction within that broader area will 
see the excessively high rain amounts and risk for flooding. 

With the forecast transitioning to a drier afternoon and much 
more active evening and overnight time period, the risk for 
severe thunderstorms has decreased. But there area still a 
handful of CAMs in both the HREF and REFS that produce UH 
tracks sufficient for severe weather during the late afternoon 
and evening from Lake Oahe to the James River Valley. If a 
storm is able to become surface-based with no inhibition late 
this afternoon, all hazards including a tornado would be 
possible. But the probability of this occurring is trending 
lower. Strong thunderstorms can still be expected though, both 
this evening through tonight and also with the first round of 
convection this morning into the early afternoon. The main 
hazard with stronger storms (aside from excessive rain and 
lightning) is expected to be hail up to nickel size.

Today will be cooler but humid, with highs in the upper 50s to 
upper 60s. Fog could develop across much of the area tonight 
into Tuesday morning as a surface ridge forms across western 
and north central North Dakota. Aside from morning fog and a 
few lingering early morning showers, Tuesday should be dry and 
sunnier with highs returning to the upper 60s to upper 70s. Dry 
weather continues on Wednesday as a deepening trough over 
central Canada pushes a cooler air mass down from the north. 
The timing of this cold front has sped up from previous 
forecasts, with highs across the north now only projected to 
reach the lower to mid 60s on Wednesday. The Wednesday night 
low temperature forecast has also cooled, with widespread mid 
30s to lower 40s and a potential for patchy frost to develop in 
low-lying, sheltered areas. The cooler but seasonable air mass 
could hang around until a potential clipper arrives this 
weekend, but there is some ensemble support for a brief warm up
to end the work week.
